title: What it looks like in a classroom when students know things
author: Lauren Brown
summary: Lauren Brown uses a former eighth-grade student, Hank, a World War I enthusiast who blurted out "Armistice Day!" when she introduced Veterans Day, to argue that background knowledge changes a whole class and not just the student who has it. She notes that knowledgeable students ask the questions and make the analogies, such as comparing blame for the Archduke's assassination to blame on Afghanistan after 9/11, that deepen discussion and get classmates thinking. She then contrasts a class period with no Hanks, bright and likeable students who simply knew little history, where she had to spend time explaining background, discussions stalled and off-task behaviour rose. The cause was not the students but the content they had not been taught in earlier grades. Her conclusion is that skipping social studies and science in the elementary years carries real costs that show up later, for every child in the room.
points: Knowledge is a classroom resource: a few knowledgeable students raise the quality of questions and discussion for everyone.
A class where nobody has the background forces the teacher to explain context and loses the back-and-forth that drives engagement.
Gaps traced to earlier grades are a curriculum problem, not a fault of the students.
Elementary social studies and science content are prerequisites for middle and high school learning.
quotes: Thinking about Hank reminds me how important knowledge is in learning. As the science of reading shows us, the more knowledge we have about a topic, the easier it is to read and learn more about.
The amazing thing about Hank, and other students who share a strong knowledge base, is the kind of questions and comments they raise that transform a class.
Maybe Austria-Hungary blaming Serbia for the assassination of Ferdinand is kinda like how we blamed Afghanistan for 9/11 cuz they were letting al-Qaeda hang out there?

And while we can argue whether, in fact, the war in Afghanistan was kinda like the start of World War I or not, the point is that such a question raises more questions and issues and gets students thinking, which is the whole point of school.
I recently realized the reason why: there were no Hanks. There were not even kids who were kind of like Hank.

The lack of knowledge made it hard to have good discussions and get through activities. I had to spend too much time explaining background info in order for students to comprehend the topic at hand. There was no one to ask interesting questions that took us deeper into the material. There was less back and forth, less engagement, and more off-task behaviors.

The consequences of not teaching content—social studies, science and other topics—in grade school are real. Students need that content in grade school to be able to learn more in middle school, high school and beyond.
And if no one else in the class knows anything, trust me, they won’t learn as much as the kids in a class period where there is more knowledge.
